Title: Coins and Change
Content: From the humble `text(penny)` to the heftier quarter, over the `text(centuries)` many changes were made to how coins look and to the materials used.

The United States `text(first)` began minting its own money in `1793`. Some of the nation’s `text(first)` minted coins intended for circulation were copper `text(cents)`. They took a long time to make using machines powered by horses and people. Silver and gold coins worth higher amounts were also created. The U.S. Mint could not produce enough coins, so Congress allowed foreign coins to be used in the United States.

The metals used in different coins have changed over time. For example, when `text(pennies)` were `text(first)` minted, they were made of copper. But copper is an expensive metal, so gradually `text(pennies)` were minted from various mixtures of metals. During `text(one year)` of World War `text(II)`, `text(pennies)` were made of steel with a zinc covering due to a copper shortage. Today, `text(pennies)` are made of the more affordable zinc with copper plating.
The End of Silver and Gold

Some coins, such as the `text(dime)` and the `text(quarter)`, are silver in color. However, they no longer contain any actual silver. The cost of silver is too high for using in coins. Instead, these coins are made of a metal mixture, or alloy, consisting mostly of copper with some nickel, which is very resistant to corrosion. In `1866`, a coin worth `text(five cents)` was made and named after the metal from which it was made — the nickel. The `text(one-dollar)` coin used to be a silver `text(dollar)`. Currently, it looks golden, but it is mostly made of copper. Gold stopped being used in coins during the Great Depression to stabilize gold prices.

Despite the use of less-expensive metals and alloys, it still costs more to make `text(pennies)` and `text(nickels)` than they are worth. Although there are periodic campaigns to discontinue some coins due to their production costs, coins continue to be made, circulated, and collected.
